Our results provide a performance adjustment spectrum to help developers make informed decisions about this new isolation standard. Our code is available on GitHub.

A substantial body of evidence suggests that the rate of star formation in galaxies peaks at an intermediate mass of approximately 10^9.5 M$_{\sun}$ before declining for more massive galaxies. One possible explanation for this downturn involves the transformation of galaxies with high specific star formation rates into quiescent ones through the growth of a bulge. To investigate this transformation process, we conducted a detailed analysis of 8000 local galaxies, taking into account both their overall size and central size. Our findings indicate that a bulge's growth is the primary factor contributing to the downturn in the SFR-main sequence for massive galaxies. Moreover, we observed that the rate of star formation in bulks and central regions of galaxies exhibits a peak at an intermediate mass of approximately 10^9.5 M$_{\sun}$ before declining for more massive galaxies. Our results are consistent with the picture of star formation occurring preferentially on the periphery of large galaxies, and the bulge's growth playing a crucial role in the formation of massive elliptical galaxies. Our findings also support the idea that the bulge formation process is closely tied to the metallicity evolution of galaxies. Our data and its analysis are available in an electronic format.
